title: Your electricity bill
blurb: Who pays for the grid that serves a datacenter, and what the record says about household rates.
why: A datacenter can draw as much power as a city. Someone pays for the wires, the substations and the new plants that serve it. When those costs are spread across all customers, the bill moves for everyone, including people who never use the service.
The record on this is thinner than it should be, but where a regulator or auditor has put a number on it, the number is in the ledger. Where only a promise exists, that is in the ledger too.
ask: Who pays for the connection?

Ask the utility commission docket whether large-load customers carry their own transmission and generation costs, or whether they are socialised. Ohio and Ontario have written minimum-payment rules; most places have not.
What is in the capacity auction?
In regions with a capacity market, the market monitor's report says how much of the clearing price is attributable to datacenter load. That is the closest thing to a receipt for a bill increase.
What did the auditor say?
Legislative auditors in Virginia and Georgia have modelled bill impacts and jobs. Those reports are public and quote a dollar range.

title: Water
blurb: How much a site takes, from which basin, and whether anyone outside the company has seen the number.
why: Most datacenters cool with water because it is cheap. Evaporative cooling in a dry basin takes drinking water out of the ground and sends it into the air. Air cooling uses more electricity and no water. Which one a site uses is a design choice, and it is usually only disclosed when a court or a council forces it.

The ledger holds the cases where the number got out: The Dalles after a lawsuit, Uruguay after a court order, Chile after an environmental tribunal, Middenmeer after a municipal audit. It also holds the designs that changed afterwards.
ask: What does the water permit say?
Withdrawal permits are public in most jurisdictions. The permitted volume is the ceiling; ask for metered use against it.
What is the basin's status?
A permit in a stressed or over-allocated basin is a different fact from the same permit in a wet one. Basin stress data is published by water agencies and by WRI Aqueduct.
Is it 'water positive'?
That phrase means the company funds water projects somewhere, not that the site takes less. Ask for the site's own withdrawal and where the offset projects are.

title: What actually burns
blurb: Gas plants, diesel generators and turbines attached to sites that are described as clean.
why: A company can buy renewable certificates for every hour it runs and still be served, physically, by a gas plant built for it. The certificate is an accounting instrument. The plant is in the utility's filing and the air permit.

The clearest records in the ledger are permits: a 944 MW gas peaker approved in Virginia, 15 turbines permitted in Memphis after a year of unpermitted running, 41 more across the state line, a 1.2 GW gas build in Wisconsin, Entergy's plants for one site in Louisiana. Each sits beside the operator's public statement about the same site.
ask: What does the air permit list?
Every site must permit its backup generators. The permitted capacity is the truest public number for how big a site is, and it often comes out before any announcement.
What is in the interconnection queue?
Grid operators publish what is waiting to connect and, for generators, what fuel. Load growth with gas attached shows up here first.
Is the renewable claim hourly?
Annual matching means buying certificates equal to annual use. Hourly matching means the clean power was there when the load was. Ask which, and whether a third party checked it.

title: The grid queue
blurb: How much is asking to connect, how much actually has, and what regulators have done about the gap.
why: Across every region with public data, the amount of datacenter load asking to connect is many times what is actually connected: roughly 60 times in Texas, 23 times in the Paris region, 14 times contracted versus real load in Malaysia. Most of it will never be built. But grids plan, and sometimes build, against the queue.

The response differs by country and the ledger records each: Ireland requires sites to bring their own dispatchable supply, Singapore paused and then rationed, Israel froze applications, Texas ordered an audit, Amsterdam tightened its cap. These are the policy levers that exist today.
ask: Queued versus connected?
Ask the grid operator for both numbers. The ratio is the fact that matters.
Who carries the risk of cancellation?
If a utility builds for a queue that evaporates, ask the commission docket who pays for the stranded capacity.
Is there a connection policy?
Ireland's and Ontario's rules are written down. Ask whether your regulator has one, and what it requires of large loads.

title: Public money and jobs
blurb: Tax exemptions, subsidies and the jobs promised in exchange, as audited.
why: Datacenters are among the most subsidised buildings on earth and among the least staffed. A hyperscale campus can receive hundreds of millions in sales-tax exemptions and employ a few dozen people once built. The job figures in announcements usually count construction and 'indirect' jobs; the audited figures count what is on site.

The ledger records the audits: Virginia's $928 million annual exemption cost, Georgia's auditor cutting its own job estimate by 70% while the cost stood, Brazil's official R$7 billion tax expenditure with no job commitment attached.
ask: What does the incentive agreement require?
Ask for the signed agreement and whether it names a jobs number, a wage floor and a clawback. Many do not.
What did the auditor find?
State and national auditors review these programmes. Their reports are the only independent count of jobs and cost.
Permanent jobs per megawatt?
Divide the on-site jobs figure by the site's capacity. It is usually well under one job per megawatt.

title: Land, noise and neighbours
blurb: Hectares taken, habitat conditions, and the noise that does not show up in a dBA reading.
why: A campus takes hundreds of hectares of farmland or green belt, runs cooling fans and generators around the clock, and sits next to people. Planning records are where land take, biodiversity conditions and noise limits are written down, and where the conditions are either enforceable or decorative.

The ledger holds both kinds: an enforceable 135% biodiversity net gain condition in England, a 2,100-acre rezoning voided by a court in Virginia, a state land sale refused in the Netherlands, a noise ordinance in Arizona that mandates studies nobody has published.
ask: How many hectares, and what was it before?
The planning application states land take. Compare it with the previous land use and any protected designation.
Is the biodiversity condition enforceable?
A condition with monitoring and a named enforcement body is different from a commitment in a design statement.
What does the noise limit measure?
Most ordinances cap dBA. The complaints are usually about low-frequency tonal noise, which dBA does not capture. Ask whether the standard addresses it.

title: What good looks like
blurb: Sites and rules where the record shows a practice worth copying, with the numbers to prove it.
why: A datacenter is a heater that computes. Its waste heat can warm a city if a pipe network exists and someone requires the connection. It can run on geothermal or hydro where those exist. It can be air-cooled where water is scarce. None of this is exotic; all of it is documented somewhere in this ledger with a published figure.

The pattern in the good cases is the same: a public owner or a binding rule, and a number that someone outside the company reports. Stockholm's half-municipal utility publishes recovered heat in its annual report. Denmark made surplus-heat analysis mandatory. Uruguay's court order produced a redesign that cut stated water use by 99%.
ask: Who owns the heat network?
Municipal or regulated networks publish delivered MWh. Private arrangements usually do not.
Is heat reuse required?
Germany and Denmark have written it into law with thresholds. Ask whether your jurisdiction has, and whether the register is public.
Is the clean supply firm and additional?
A geothermal or hydro allocation with a regulator's order behind it is different from an annual certificate purchase.

title: The hardware chain
blurb: The mines, the fabs, the people who work them, and where the servers go when they die.
why: A GPU is cobalt from Congo, copper from Chile, nickel from Indonesia, rare earths from Myanmar, gallium from China, water from Taiwan, and labour at every step. Three to five years later it is e-waste, and the world formally collects less than a quarter of what it generates. The rest is tracked, when it is tracked at all, by GPS beacons hidden in discarded equipment.

This end of the ledger is the least documented and the most important, because it is where the cost gets exported to places with the weakest records. It holds what the UN, the USGS, the Basel Convention and national regulators have published, and it says plainly where nothing has.
ask: Is the mineral sourcing traced to the mine?
Statutory conflict-minerals filings cover tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold. They do not cover cobalt, nickel or rare earths. Ask what covers those.
How long does the hardware live?
Companies state depreciation lives in their annual filings. Ask what happens to a GPU at the end of that period, and whether the reuse figure is third-party assured.
Where does the e-waste go?
Compare the national Basel report with customs data for used electronics. The gap between them is the undeclared flow.
